latin.671: XI. Quinta postremaque Clarissimi Professoris Probatio, in eo desierat, in quo prima cœperat, nempe, in Ignoratione Elenchi, opponendô Reformatis, Oralem corporis Christi Manducationem impugnantibus, Irenæi verba, quibus S. Cœnam ex duabus rebus, cœlesti & terrena, constare docetur, Reformatorum Confessionibus Sendomiriensi, Toruniensi aliísque inserta, tanquam talia, quæ ambabus ulnis amplectuntur Reformati.
latin.672: Nihilominus Vindicatio, quâ Autor hanc Elenchi aberrationem suam obvelare studet §. XIX, ejusdem, imô deterioris, commatis est, unam duabus aliis cumulans, quando Reformatos ab Irenæi mente & verbis secessisse confirmare conatur, quarum una à Subjectô Quæstionis, altera à Prædicato deviat: A Subjecto aberrat, dum Reformatorum in locum, unicum Calvinum substituit; quasi verò Reformati & Calvinus nomina essent Synonyma, vel termini convertibiles.
latin.673: Quanquam Calvinum quà rem cum Irenæo amicissimè conspirare fusissimè evincunt Guilielmus Forbes. Reformatus, & Johannes Fabricius, Lutheranus; Quæ autem in contrarium à Calvino edita apparent, facile conciliantur Distinctione inter Præsentiam corporis Christi in Cœna Spiritualem, & Corporalem seu Localem, quarum priorem cum Irenæo admittit Calvinus, posteriorem, cum universa Antiquitate, rejicit, cum eadem constantissimè professus, corpus Christi corporali localíque modo tantùm in cælo, non autem vel in Cœna, vel ubique esse.
latin.674: A Prædicato aberrat, dum Irenæi alia nonnulla, Valentinianis opposita, Reformatis opponit, non solum nullibi à me adducta, & ad rem de qua quæritur, scil. Num doctrina de Orali manducatione, Fidei Christianæ fundamentalis sit? nullo modo pertinentia, sed prætereà Reformatis itidem plenissime admissa: Quemadmodum enim Reformati cum Irenæo Eucharistiam ex duabus partibus constare ajunt.
latin.675: Sic etiam corpora nostra, i.e. fidelium, tam Eucharistiam, i.e. panem Eucharisticum, percipere, quàm percipientia, jam non amplius corruptibilia esse, sed spem resurrectionis ad vitam æternam habentia, profitentur. At aliud est, corpora fidelium Eucharistiam percipere; aliud, Ore corporis, corpus Christi manducare; Iterúmque: aliud, corpora fidelium Eucharistiam percipientia, non corruptibilia esse, vel, in morte mansura, sed spem resurrectionis habere; aliud (quomodo Autor Irenæum interpretatur) corpora nostra corruptibilia, corpore & sanguine Christi incorruptibilibus, nutriri & ali, hôcque pacto incorruptibilia fieri.
latin.676: Quomodo enim (quærit Autor circa finem Paragraphi XIX, Elenchi Ignorationem petitione principii adaucturus) incorruptio maneat caro, quæ à corpore Domini & sanguine, velut ab arbore vitæ, alitur & sustentatur? Quodsi verò Auctor genuinam causam Incorruptibilitatis corporum eorum, quæ dignè Eucharistiam perceperunt, & unde resurrectionis spem indepta sint, cognoscere cupit, ex ipsius Christi ore istud intelligat, non corporalem corporis Christi Manducationem, eam esse, sed Spiritualem Animarum, de qua, & quidem sola, ex hypothesi Autoris, ita Christus Joh. 6. Qui manducat Carnem meam & bibit sanguinem meum, hoc ipso habet vitam æternam, putà quà corpus, non quà animam, namque suscitabo eum in die novissimo, vers. 54.

pass_a.671: XI. The Fifth and last Proof of the most distinguished Professor had ended where the first began, namely in Ignoratio Elenchi — opposing to the Reformed, who attack Oral Eating of Christ’s body, Irenaeus’s words teaching that the Holy Supper consists of two things, heavenly and earthly, inserted in the Reformed Sendomirian, Torunian, and other Confessions, as such as the Reformed embrace with both arms.
pass_a.672: Nevertheless the Vindication by which the Author tries to veil this elenchus aberration of his in §. XIX is of the same, indeed a worse, stamp, piling one on two others, when he tries to confirm that the Reformed have seceded from Irenaeus’s mind and words, of which one wanders from the Subject of the Question, the other from the Predicate: He wanders from the Subject when he substitutes Calvin alone in place of the Reformed — as if Reformed and Calvin were synonymous names or convertible terms.
pass_a.673: Although that Calvin most amicably conspires with Irenaeus as to the matter, William Forbes the Reformed and Johannes Fabricius the Lutheran most fully prove; and what appears published contrary by Calvin is easily reconciled by the Distinction between Spiritual presence of Christ’s body in the Supper and Corporal or Local — of which Calvin admits the former with Irenaeus, rejects the latter with all Antiquity, having with the same most constantly professed that Christ’s body in a corporal and local mode is only in heaven, not in the Supper or everywhere.
pass_a.674: He wanders from the Predicate when he opposes to the Reformed some other sayings of Irenaeus against the Valentinians — not only nowhere adduced by me, and in no way pertaining to the matter inquired after (whether the doctrine of Oral eating is fundamental to Christian Faith), but moreover likewise most fully admitted by the Reformed: For just as the Reformed with Irenaeus affirm that the Eucharist consists of two parts.
pass_a.675: So also they profess that our bodies — i.e. of the faithful — both receive the Eucharist (i.e. the Eucharistic bread) and, receiving, are no longer merely corruptible but have hope of resurrection to eternal life. But it is one thing for the faithful’s bodies to receive the Eucharist; another to eat Christ’s body with the mouth of the body. Again: one thing that bodies receiving the Eucharist are not (merely) corruptible or to remain in death but have resurrection hope; another (as the Author interprets Irenaeus) that our corruptible bodies are nourished and fed by Christ’s incorruptible body and blood and thereby made incorruptible.
pass_a.676: For how (asks the Author near the end of Paragraph XIX, about to swell Ignoratio Elenchi with petitio principii) does incorruption remain in flesh fed and sustained by the Lord’s body and blood as by the tree of life? But if the Author wants the genuine cause of incorruptibility of bodies that worthily received the Eucharist and whence they obtained resurrection hope, let him learn it from Christ’s own mouth: it is not corporal Eating of Christ’s body, but Spiritual Eating of souls — of which alone, on the Author’s own hypothesis, Christ speaks in John 6: Who eats my Flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life — namely as to the body, not as to the soul — for I will raise him up on the last day, v. 54.

671: §.XI: the Professor’s fifth and last proof ends where the first began — Ignoratio Elenchi.
He sets Irenaeus’s “two things, heavenly and earthly” (in Sendomir, Toruń, and other Reformed confessions the Reformed gladly embrace) against those who deny Oral eating of Christ’s body.
672: His §.XIX vindication only worsens the miss: he piles new slips while claiming the Reformed left Irenaeus’s mind and words.
Subject error: he swaps Calvin alone for “the Reformed,” as if Reformed and Calvin were one name.
673: Forbes (Reformed) and Fabricius (Lutheran) show Calvin agrees with Irenaeus on the matter.

Apparent clashes resolve by spiritual vs corporal/local presence: Calvin with Irenaeus keeps the spiritual; with all antiquity he rejects corporal/local presence in the Supper or everywhere — body only in heaven that way.
674: Predicate error: he aims Irenaeus’s anti-Valentinian lines at the Reformed — texts Strimesius never cited, and irrelevant to whether Oral eating is faith-fundamental.
The Reformed fully admit them anyway, and with Irenaeus say the Eucharist consists of two parts.
675: They also teach the faithful’s bodies receive the Eucharistic bread and, receiving, hold resurrection hope — no longer merely corruptible.

But receiving the Eucharist ≠ orally eating Christ’s body; and resurrection hope for receivers ≠ the Author’s reading that corruptible bodies are fed into incorruption by Christ’s incorruptible body and blood.
676: Near §.XIX’s end the Author asks how flesh stays incorrupt if fed by the Lord’s body and blood as by the tree of life — stacking petitio principii on Ignoratio Elenchi.

The real cause, from Christ’s mouth, is not corporal eating but Spiritual eating of souls alone (Jn 6:54: eat my Flesh, drink my blood — eternal life as to the body; I will raise him). Stop §.XI before §.XII.
